comments.body:
PLAN REVIEW #1: BLOCK, two findings (G6 and T8), same root cause, and both were RIGHT.

I wrote that REBAR_LLM_CONFIG_FILE 'LAYERS per-key over the discovered config' and never said at what
DEPTH. The reviewer grounded it in the actual code: read_reserved_section (config.py:588-600) does
merged.update(sub) — a SHALLOW merge. Under that, an operator who overrides only frontier.model in CI
silently LOSES their project's frontier.provider, endpoint and fallback chain, because the whole
frontier sub-table is replaced. And a fallback chain, being a TOML array-of-tables, gets clobbered
rather than merged. So the plan's own stated purpose — 'an environment overriding one key does not
have to restate the whole config' — was contradicted by the only discovery mechanism it planned to
use. Neither triage bucket flagged it (all 11 were 'defer'); this came from the criteria the plan
opted into.

RESOLVED, now stated as a decision in the Approach rather than left to the implementer:

- Tables merge RECURSIVELY, leaf key wins. Anything shallower defeats the purpose.
- Arrays REPLACE wholesale, never append. Rejected append because a chain that can only grow can
  never be shortened, reordered, or cleared — CI could not pin 'no fallback, fail loudly' over a
  project default. fallback = [] explicitly disables fallbacks.
- Precedence unchanged in shape: CLI -c > env > REBAR_LLM_CONFIG_FILE > discovered file > default.
- read_reserved_section is NOT changed. Its shallow merge is shared by every reserved section and
  deepening it would silently alter layering for unrelated consumers. The deep merge lives in the
  llm resolver over the section dict it receives. Any child editing read_reserved_section has
  mis-scoped the change — that is now written into the plan so an executor cannot get it wrong.

Three ACs added, each falsifiable against the shallow-merge failure mode: deep-merge preservation of
sibling keys, array-replace including the empty-array case, and an assertion that the shared helper's
behaviour is untouched for a non-llm section.

comments.body:
KEYSTONE DECISION — how a workflow step names a CLASS. Recorded on the parent because children 172e
and 7761 BOTH block on it (10 blocking findings between them, one root cause), and cc33 inherits it.

THE GAP the reviews found: f844 shipped the class system, but NOTHING can consume it from a workflow.
The v3 step schema is closed/immutable and offers only 'model:' (a literal id string) and
'model_ladder:' (a list of literal strings). There is no 'class:' key, and the reviewers correctly
refused plans that said a step should 'express the per-pass class' without saying how.

DECISION: the three class names are RESERVED VALUES in the EXISTING model-string space. No schema
change; the DSL stays closed and its VALUE space gains three reserved words.

    model: standard                                  # was: model: claude-sonnet-4-6
    model_ladder: [trivial, standard, frontier]      # was: three literal ids

Resolution happens at the ONE funnel every step model already passes through —
config.resolve_model(cfg, step=, workflow=) at config.py:347, today literally
'return step or workflow or cfg.model'. If the resolved string is one of trivial/standard/frontier,
resolve it through model_classes.load_class_slots(); otherwise return it unchanged. A literal id
keeps working byte-for-byte, so every existing workflow YAML is unaffected and the migration is
opt-in per step.

WHY NOT a new 'class:' key: it would fork the step schema (which runs.py documents as closed), force
every consumer to handle two mutually exclusive keys, and make 'model: standard' vs 'class: standard'
a silent ambiguity. Reserved values keep ONE resolution path.

WHY NOT resolve at YAML load time: the class -> id mapping depends on env/CLI layers that are
process-scoped, so a load-time resolution would freeze the wrong value in a long-lived process and
would not be visible to provider_provenance (343b).

COLLATERAL, and 7761's reviewer is right to flag it: sizing.MODEL_LADDER (sizing.py:99-103) hardcodes
the three BARE Anthropic names with their context windows, and models_at_or_above() returns those
names for runtime escalation. Its lookup is a SUBSTRING match ('if n in model'), so it happens to
match a Bedrock id like bedrock:us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6 — but it RETURNS the bare Anthropic
name, so a Bedrock run that escalates would silently jump to DIRECT ANTHROPIC opus. That is a second
split-brain, distinct from the entry-rung one 7761 already names, and it must be fixed in the same
change or the cutover leaks cross-provider on every escalation.

SCOPE NOTE: this is specifying an unspecified mechanism, not redesigning the approved model. The
three-class model, the per-class provider/model/endpoint, the fallback chains and the layering
pointer are unchanged.

CORRECTION to the keystone decision — my 'ONE funnel' claim was WRONG, and 172e's review caught it
with three independent findings. Verified each myself before rewriting.

WHAT I GOT WRONG: I said class names would be resolved at config.resolve_model because every step
model passes through it. Three things are false about that.

1. config.py CANNOT call model_classes at module level. model_classes.py imports FROM config.py and
   its own docstring — which I wrote — says 'config.py must never import this module back'. I
   proposed the exact cycle I had prohibited one ticket earlier.
2. model_ladder BYPASSES resolve_model entirely. VERIFIED: production_batch_runner.py:93 does
    and code_review/batch_runner.py:55
   does . Ladder rungs travel through BatchRunRequest straight to the
   runners and never touch resolve_model.
3. The verifier paths bypass it too. resolve_verifier_model (verify.py:269) is its own path, and
   _verifier_cfg (plan_review/__init__.py:46) is a consumer with TWO further call sites at
   xcheck.py:198 and :336 that no plan had enumerated.

CORRECTED MECHANISM — one FUNCTION, three CALL SITES (not one funnel):

  model_classes.resolve_model_string(value: str) -> str
      if value in ('trivial','standard','frontier'): resolve via load_class_slots()
      else: return value unchanged

Called at exactly three places:
  a. config.resolve_model            — via a LAZY, function-level import. This does not create a
                                       module-level cycle, and it is the established pattern in
                                       this file already (config.py:108, :566, :768 all do it).
  b. the ladder expansion            — production_batch_runner.py:93 and code_review/batch_runner.py:55
  c. the verifier path               — resolve_verifier_model, and _verifier_cfg with its xcheck.py callers

Import direction is UNCHANGED and still one-way at module scope: model_classes imports config
normally; config imports model_classes only inside a function body.

WHY ONE FUNCTION STILL MATTERS even without one funnel: the reserved-word vocabulary and the
class -> id resolution live in exactly one place, so the three call sites cannot drift. What I gave
up is the claim that a single interception point exists — it does not, and pretending otherwise
would have left ladders and verifiers silently unresolved while the tests on the step path passed.

The USER-FACING syntax is unchanged:  and 
still work exactly as decided; only the internal wiring is corrected.

compiled_state.description:
# Model classes: trivial / standard / frontier as the universal LLM interface

## Context / Problem

rebar's gates deliberately run different model tiers per pass, but the selection is not expressible
as configuration. It is INFERRED, and the inference inverts off the default provider:

- `review_kernel/verify.py:269` is `verifier_default if model == default_model else (model or
  verifier_default)`. Any model that is not the literal framework default — every Bedrock id — is
  read as an explicit operator choice, so the Pass-2/Pass-4 downgrade SILENTLY STOPS APPLYING.
- `completion.py:332` repeats the same equality test on a separate path, so the completion verifier
  loses its downgrade the same way.
- `workflow/gates/code-review.yaml` declares no `model:` on any step, so ALL FOUR of code review's
  passes take `cfg.model` and it never downgrades at all.
- `plan-review.yaml:62-65` sets `model_ladder` to BARE names (`claude-haiku-4-5`,
  `claude-sonnet-4-6`, `claude-opus-4-8`), and `config.py:333-341` maps the prefix `claude` to
  provider `anthropic`. So on a Bedrock run the Pass-1 finders still resolve to DIRECT ANTHROPIC —
  a split-brain in the pass that does most of the work (MEASURED on a real review: 41 of 42 calls).

The root cause is one knob for four passes. `REBAR_LLM_MODEL` is a single scalar, and a scalar cannot
express a per-tier mapping. That is also why `REBAR_LLM_BEDROCK_MODEL_ID` was deleted
[rebar:281f-3336-c668-4979] — a second scalar does not help.

## Approach

Introduce THREE capability classes — `trivial`, `standard`, `frontier` — as the universal interface
every rebar LLM call site resolves against. Each class is a config SLOT the operator fills with a
model/provider/endpoint (and an optional fallback chain); rebar's internals reference the class, never
a model id.

**Prior art (this shape is not invented).** LiteLLM's proxy config is exactly this: a `model_list` of
`{model_name: <alias>, litellm_params: {model, api_base, api_key, ...}}` plus
`router_settings.fallbacks` mapping alias -> [alias]. Callers reference the alias; deployment details
and failover live in config. Aider solves the same problem role-wise (`--model` / `--weak-model` /
`--editor-model`, with each main model carrying a default weak model). pydantic-ai supplies the
runtime half but no config schema: `FallbackModel(default, *fallbacks, fallback_on=...)` takes model
instances or `provider:model` strings, so rebar constructs one per class from config.

**Rebar already thinks in these tiers**, which is why the axis is right: `DEFAULT_MODEL` is the
frontier model and `VERIFIER_DEFAULT_MODEL` is documented in-code as "the decisive NON-FRONTIER
model". This formalizes a distinction the code already makes implicitly.

**Alternative rejected — a second scalar (`REBAR_LLM_VERIFIER_MODEL`).** It fixes only the verifier
half, leaves the Pass-1 ladder routing to Anthropic, and would be a config surface we ship and then
deprecate once classes land. Rejected as knowingly short-lived.

**Alternative rejected — provider-qualifying the ladder in the gate YAML.** Most explicit, but it
hard-codes one provider into the gate definition, which is exactly what makes today's ladder
non-portable.

**Config shape.** The three names are SLOTS the client fills, not presets rebar ships and the client
selects. Nothing requires the operator to know rebar's internal vocabulary beyond the three slot
names:

    [tool.rebar.llm.frontier]
    model = "us.anthropic.claude-opus-4-8"
    provider = "bedrock"

    [[tool.rebar.llm.trivial.fallback]]
    model = "us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5"
    provider = "bedrock"

Secrets are NOT part of this structure. rebar's config layer deliberately keeps API keys env-only
(`config.py:388-398` states secrets are not config-file keys); LiteLLM puts `api_key` inline in
`litellm_params` and rebar must not copy that.

**Config discovery is unchanged**, with one addition: `REBAR_LLM_CONFIG_FILE` names a file that
LAYERS over the discovered config (pyproject `[tool.rebar.llm]` / `rebar.toml` / XDG). It layers
rather than replaces so an environment overriding one key does not have to restate the whole config
— duplication is the likelier source of drift than precedence subtlety. No new discovery path is
invented; the pointer IS the escape hatch.

**The merge is DEEP over tables and REPLACING over arrays.** This is the decision, not a preference:

- **Tables merge recursively, leaf key wins.** Setting only `frontier.model` in the pointed-to file
  keeps the discovered `frontier.provider`, `frontier.endpoint` and `frontier.fallback`. Anything
  shallower defeats the stated purpose — a table-level replace would force CI to restate an entire
  class slot to change one field, which IS the duplication this pointer exists to avoid.
- **Arrays are replaced wholesale, never appended.** A `fallback` chain in the pointed-to file
  REPLACES the discovered chain; `fallback = []` explicitly disables fallbacks. Appending is
  rejected because a chain that can only grow can never be shortened, reordered, or cleared by an
  environment — CI could not pin "no fallback, fail loudly" over a project default.
- **Precedence, unchanged in shape:** CLI `-c` > env > `REBAR_LLM_CONFIG_FILE` > discovered config
  file > built-in default. The pointer slots directly above the discovered file. Secrets stay
  env-only at every layer.

**This does NOT change `read_reserved_section`.** That helper's `merged.update(sub)`
(`config.py:588-600`) is a SHALLOW merge shared by every reserved section, and deepening it would
silently alter layering for unrelated consumers. The deep merge is implemented in the llm config
resolver over the section dict it receives, leaving the shared helper's contract untouched. Any
child that finds itself editing `read_reserved_section` has mis-scoped the change.

**`REBAR_LLM_MODEL` is DEPRECATED with a migration window** rather than kept as a permanent alias.
There are few clients today and a single-scalar knob alongside a class model is precisely the
ambiguity this work removes.

## Scope

This parent's contract, delivered by its children:

- `src/rebar/llm/config.py` — the three class slots, their parsing from the existing layered config,
  and the class resolver.
- `src/rebar/llm/config.py` / `_config_sources.py` — the `REBAR_LLM_CONFIG_FILE` pointer and its
  per-key layering.
- `src/rebar/llm/review_kernel/verify.py`, `src/rebar/llm/completion.py`,
  `src/rebar/llm/workflow/gates/code-review.yaml` — the three verifier paths resolve `standard`
  instead of inferring from an equality test.
- `src/rebar/llm/workflow/gates/plan-review.yaml` and the batch runners — the Pass-1 ladder is
  expressed in classes, not bare model names.
- `src/rebar/llm/` — per-class fallback chains constructed as pydantic-ai `FallbackModel`.
- `src/rebar/llm/config.py`, `docs/` — the `REBAR_LLM_MODEL` deprecation, an ADR, and example configs
  per provider.

## Testing

Unit tier for resolution and layering (pure config, no model calls); contract tier for the gate
paths (the observable is which model id each pass resolves to); and one live [operator-attested]
run for the end-to-end claim. Per-child tiers are stated on each child.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] every child ticket is closed
- [ ] a test asserts the pointed-to file DEEP-merges tables: a file setting only `frontier.model`
      over a discovered config carrying `frontier.provider` + a `frontier.fallback` chain yields the
      overridden model AND the discovered provider and fallback chain (the shallow-merge failure
      mode drops them, so this test fails against `dict.update` semantics)
- [ ] a test asserts arrays REPLACE rather than append: a `fallback` chain in the pointed-to file
      yields exactly that chain, and `fallback = []` yields no fallbacks
- [ ] a test asserts `read_reserved_section`'s own shallow-merge behaviour is UNCHANGED for a
      non-llm reserved section, so the deep merge did not leak into shared config machinery
- [ ] a test asserts each of the three verifier paths (plan-review Pass-2/Pass-4, completion) resolves
      the `standard` class rather than inferring from an equality against the framework default
- [ ] a test asserts no bare `claude-*` id resolves to provider `anthropic` during a run whose classes
      are configured for another provider
- [ ] [operator-attested] a real gate run with classes configured across two providers records the
      per-pass model ids actually used, cited from the run's usage log in a comment
